title: Black Patti and the Melrose recording session
summary: He recalls recording Boar Hog Blues and Squeeze Me for Black Patti, and a Melrose session that ended when he refused to change the trombone note.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Yeah. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Yeah. No, he was a, no, wait a minute, I can't think of the, but we cut, I cut, I think, four, four numbers, before, I made, I recorded, the boy called blues, and squeezed me. Bull Hog on one side and squeezed me is on the other.
That was on the Black Patty.

Black Patty. Now the other records that we made was for Melrose. We made them at Chicago, what is it, Chicago Avenue in the Lake, out there, 17th floor. That's where we made them. But Mr. Melrose, his brother was over there. The old Melrose wasn't there, he said.
Yes, Walter was the oldest one, wasn't he?
Yes, I think so. And the young one was the blonde head. There was Lester. Yeah. And there was the piano player, Frank Melrose.

Well, I think we did business with the heavy something, the blonde, Connie blonde had one. Mr. Melrose himself was thin, wasn't he, a little thin. Well, that's who he made these last records with until we went down there to cut full numbers, two records. And that stuff is all in storage, I couldn't give you that because I made manuscripts of the numbers. And then we was talking about it last night. And in making these numbers, he had a four-boy introduction on one. And that's the number he wanted to cut first, was his own music. And I told him in rehearsal, we were rehearsing over here on Prairie, and 52nd Street. And I told him, I said, we'll have to change that trombone number, that trombone note. And he got sold with me and said that it was his music and he wanted it like he wanted. So we went down to record this. So the man, the, he hit with us down, played with us and went on so and so with us until he told us to hit. Well, the hit made the introduction. We went on and started the first string of the number. And after we started, the man see, we knew what we had. He stopped us. He said, well, to save time, he says, you boys will have to change that trombone number, the trombone note in there. And mine got bad with him. And they had a horse. And the man went and got a sheet of paper, pencil, come back. Mine got up from the piano, grabbed his music and he said, if that's the way you want it, he says, oh, you pack up. And we came on out of the studio. We didn't make those, and he had some nice numbers. No, we had some nice numbers. Lee Collins made them. Yeah. Whatever it was, because I met somebody on 47 in Michigan after coming from the Rican and they told me Lee Collins and told me who, I think he had Dominic, Dominic and Lee Collins is the man made him.
